name: Elmo

claims.text:
The name Elmo is in Quenya. Its meaning is unclear, but it could be a combination of él (being a poetic word for star) and the suffix -mo ("person").
Elmō was also a Primitive Elvish name for the planet Venus.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: I. Dark and Light", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, Text 1B, p. 281

claims.text: Elmō was also a Primitive Elvish name for the planet Venus.

claims.text: The name Nelwë is in Quenya, but its meaning is not entirely clear. The second element of the name -wë is a suffix used mainly in masculine names of the First Age, being an old word for "person". According to Paul Strack, the first element of the name might be a derivation from the root NEL ("three").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", p. 340

claims.text: Elmo and his elder brothers were directly descended through eldest son to eldest son from Enel, the first of the Nelyar to awaken. Unlike his older brothers who had been born by the time the Elves were found by the Valar, Elmo was born during the Great Journey.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 142

claims.text: He remained behind in Beleriand after Elwë was lost in Nan Elmoth and Olwë departed for Valinor. After Elwë returned, Elmo remained with and was beloved by him.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", last paragraph before the section"Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 233

claims.text: Given that Elmo’s grandson Celeborn was reckoned a prince of Doriath, it is likely that Elmo was likewise a prince. It is unknown if he survived the sack of Doriath or what his fate was otherwise. No specific deeds are ascribed to Elmo, and he is largely notable for his descendants: Celeborn, who was one of the noble Sindar, and Nimloth, who was briefly Queen of Doriath, when she married Dior, Thingol's successor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", last paragraph before the section"Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 233

claims.text:
Elmo was developed to explain the reference in The Silmarillion that Celeborn was a "kinsman of Thingol". One of the solutions was to establish Celeborn as the son of an unimportant brother of Thingol. Depending on the texts, Elmo is considered as a younger brother of Elwë (Thingol), the grandfather of Celeborn or his father.
In a draft genealogy of Elwë and Elmo's descendants dated to December 1959 that Christopher Tolkien rejected from Unfinished Tales, Nimloth is the granddaughter of Elmo rather than great-granddaughter (sister rather than daughter of Galathil).
In other, later writings, Celeborn is a Teler of Aman rather than a Sinda of Doriath, and a grandson of Olwë rather than of Elmo. Without further revision to Galadriel's own genealogy, this origin for Celeborn would cause the couple to become first cousins. Tolkien did not develop this idea further.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVIII. Elvish Ages & Númenórean", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 148; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: V. The Tale of Years", p. 350; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", last paragraph before the section"Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 233

claims.text: In The Nature of Middle-earth there appears a character called Nelwë. There, he is presented as an ancestor of Celeborn (who was an elf of Aman in this version of his history), and a younger brother of Elwë, Olwë, and Eärwen.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: XVI. Galadriel and Celeborn", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 349

claims.text: The entire text in which he appears, however, was struck through and rejected. While it is not explicitly mentioned anywhere by Tolkien that the character of Nelwë is equivalent to that of Elmo, or otherwise the latter's literary successor, he nonetheless fulfills the same role as an ancestor of Celeborn, in which the kinship of Celeborn and Thingol is elaborated on in a more exact manner.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: XVI. Galadriel and Celeborn", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 349
